transcript.text: Hi, I've got a Dyson V15 Detect (SV22) about 4 months old. When I go from the kitchen tiles onto the lounge rug the motor suddenly gets much louder and the battery number drops faster, then it calms down again when I go back on the tiles. Also the screen goes up and down by itself. Is the motor on its way out? It's still under guarantee so I want to report it before it dies completely.

No — from that pattern alone, it does not sound like a motor that is on its way out. A V15 can alter its power demand as the floorhead moves from smooth tiles onto a rug, and its remaining-time estimate can drop and rise because it is recalculating from the power currently being used. The screen’s graph can also move as it detects differing amounts and sizes of dust, which is normal. A failing motor would more usually give a constant rough grinding, screeching or harsh whine regardless of floor type, often with loss of suction, overheating or cutting out. The main alternative is hair/debris restricting the brush bar or an airflow blockage, particularly if the change is unusually harsh or it starts pulsing. Which power mode is selected (Eco, Auto/Med or Boost), and is the screen movement the coloured bar graph/particle count or the remaining-minutes figure? If it is in Auto/Med and otherwise runs smoothly, this is very likely normal rather than a guarantee fault.

Thank you. The screen says 'Auto' - I pressed the mode button once and it went to that; the other options are Eco and Boost. The thing that moves is the remaining-minutes figure, which jumps up and down, and the particle bar chart also changes. There are no warning symbols or red lights, and no pulsing or burning smell.

That makes this sound still more like normal Auto-mode behaviour, not a failing motor. In Auto, the machine can vary power demand as conditions change; the remaining-minutes figure is an estimate based on that current demand, so it can fall on the rug and recover on tiles. The particle chart changing is also expected as the pickup changes. The only simple alternative worth ruling out is hair or fluff making the roller work harder on carpet: switch it off, remove the battery if it is readily removable, and inspect the roller and its end areas for a wrap of hair/thread. If it is clear and the noise remains a smooth change rather than a rattle, grinding or screech, there is no clear guarantee fault to report. Contact Dyson under the guarantee if it begins pulsing, loses suction, overheats/cuts out, shows a warning, or makes the same harsh noise on all surfaces.
I've looked at the brush bar and it's clean, with no hair or thread wrapped round it. Should I be worried that the noise changes by itself like that, or is it genuinely nothing to report to Dyson?

In Auto, power demand can alter as pickup conditions change, so the run-time estimate and particle graph will continually recalculate; the roller also has more resistance on a rug than on tiles. A motor problem would be more concerning if the noise were harsh, metallic, grinding or screeching, or if it began pulsing, losing suction, overheating, cutting out or showing a warning. As a final comparison, select Eco and make one pass from tiles onto the same rug: if it remains broadly smooth and steady, that supports normal Auto behaviour; if there is still an abrupt harsh noise, contact Dyson under the guarantee and describe it as a floorhead/noise issue.

I've just tried it in Eco and the sound stays the same quiet level on both the rug and the tiles. In Boost it's loud all the time and doesn't change. So is it just the Auto setting doing this? I only switched to it about two weeks ago, which is when I first noticed it.

Yes — the Eco and Boost comparison makes it very likely that this is simply Auto mode doing its job. The moving particle graph and changing time estimate fit that behaviour too. On the evidence so far, there is no sign of the motor failing and nothing you need to report as a fault to Dyson. Keep an eye on it, but contact Dyson under the guarantee if it starts making a harsh/grinding noise in Eco as well, pulses, loses suction, cuts out, overheats, or shows a warning.
